messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: rats comparisons
parts:
Hi all,

I tried running Metropolis on the rats example using various rescaled proposal distributions. The results are:
1. It takes forever to burn in without rescaling. Longer than I was willing to wait (20 minutes).
2. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use an isotropic Gaussian proposal distribution (scaled to get near .234 accept rate) you get a minimum ESS of about 40 after 1M iterations.
3. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use a Gaussian proposal distribution with diagonal covariance equal to the variance of the posterior (scaled to get near .234 accept rate), you get a minimum ESS of about 24 after 10K iterations, which is about 60x better than unscaled.
4. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use a Gaussian proposal distribution with full covariance equal to the covariance of the posterior (scaled to get near .234 accept rate), you get a minimum ESS of about 20 after 10K iterations, which is indistinguishable from diagonal covariance.

By contrast:
5. NUTS with no rescaling and good initialization gets a minimum ESS of about 500 using about 100K gradient evaluations, which is around 2x as efficient as Metropolis with good scaling.
6. NUTS with step size rescaling (equivalent to diagonal covariance for Metropolis) gets a minimum ESS of about 500 using about 7K gradient evaluations, which is about 30x as efficient as Metropolis with good scaling.
(These comparisons ignore the extra cost of gradient evaluations, which is sort of cheating.)

Finally:
7. JAGS gets about 3300 effective samples using 10K sweeps, which is about 4-5x as efficient as rescaled NUTS.
(This comparison ignores possible differences between the cost of gradient evaluations and the cost of Gibbs sweeps.)

So in summary, here's a Girolami and Calderhead style table:

Sampler                Normalized ESS
raw Metropolis         1
diagonal Metropolis    60
full-cov Metropolis    50
raw NUTS               125
rescaled NUTS          1785
JAGS                   8250

If we took away the model's conjugacy, JAGS would get hit by a pretty big penalty for reverting to slice sampling. I'd guess a factor of 10–20, which would make its performance worse than rescaled NUTS. So that's encouraging.

Matt

PS: This evaluation assumes we already know the covariance matrix of the target distribution, and discounts any additional cost involved in finding it during burn-in/inefficiencies before we've found it. Which is probably a big deal.

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rats comparisons
parts:
It's a little surprising, I agree. It might have something to do with the Radfordian argument about random walks over the range of values of the log-posterior probability. For this model, the log-posterior probability (hereafter referred to as logp) has a range of about 25. In section 5.4.4 of Radford's HMC chapter, he argues that if you've got a target distribution whose variables are i.i.d., then Metropolis kernels that are tuned to a .234 acceptance rate should produce proposals whose changes in logp are approximately normally distributed with mean -2.8 and variance 5.6. If you simulate the resulting process (including rejections), then it can actually take hundreds of iterations to cover a range of 25.

But I'm not sure there isn't a flaw in my (interpretation of Radford's) reasoning. So I ran 10K Metropolis steps on a 65-dimensional (like the rats example) standard normal distribution with jumps tuned to get about .23 acceptance probability, and got a min ESS of about 25. Which is pretty damn close to 1/500. So it looks like that's about as good as it's possible for Metropolis to do for a target distribution with this dimensionality, since it doesn't get much easier than an isotropic normal. (Metropolis would do better in terms of ESS/sweep if you ran it on each dimension independently for this example. But maybe not in terms of ESS/function evaluation.)

Matt

parts: PPS: There was a bug in the way I was learning the rescaling parameters for NUTS before, which is why it wasn't helping. When you do it right, it totally works, unsurprisingly. But it can get into big trouble if you start rescaling during burn-in, since the "standard deviations" are actually just a measure of how badly you initialized the parameters and don't relate at all to the proper scale. This could be fixed by 1. doing a better job of initializing, e.g. using an optimizer or 2. something else, like maybe estimating the standard deviations using mini batches that throw away previous mini batches completely.

Variances aren't hard to estimate, but the catch is that you need to be in the stationary regime before you start estimating them or else all hell breaks loose as you can get into a loop where you have tiny step sizes for some dimensions, and so you don't make any progress in those dimensions, so you estimate that the variance in those dimensions is even tinier, etc. This might be partly a result of normalizing the scales—I'm going to try cutting that part out.

I bet we could make a nice scaling with dimensionality graph for the bugs examples. We can put wall-clock efficiency versus dimensionality on a log-log plot, with each point being a model/sampler. If we normalize it so that e.g. NUTS's performance is the x-axis, we can compare slopes and intercepts. Intercepts capture implementation overhead and anything that's badly tuned for the problem. Slopes capture scaling with dimension, so unscaled Metropolis should have a slope of -1 and anything that does matrix inversions should have a slope of -2. (Gibbs might be all over the map.)

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rats comparisons
parts:
It's not that you aren't moving at all, it's that you aren't moving in specific dimensions. If you're underestimating the appropriate scale for some dimension at 1/1000th of what it should be, then you'll make progress in all of the other dimensions but not in that one. So basically you're doing anti-Gibbs. Tuning acceptance rates works as usual, because you still need to reject moves in the other dimensions. But it takes a long long time to figure out that you've radically underestimated the scale of one of the dimensions, because you're moving so slowly in that dimension.

I've been tuning the sum of the scales, not the determinant—it could be that the determinant (or geometric mean for diagonal scaling) is a better choice. But regardless of how we measure overall scale this problem can still come up if we do a really bad job of estimating relative scales initially, e.g., because we're using samples along the trajectory from the initial state to the target high-mass region to estimate standard deviations.

On Nov 19, 2011, at 9:52 AM, Matt Hoffman wrote:

> It's not that you aren't moving at all, it's that you aren't moving in specific dimensions. If you're underestimating the appropriate scale for some dimension at 1/1000th of what it should be, then you'll make progress in all of the other dimensions but not in that one. So basically you're doing anti-Gibbs. Tuning acceptance rates works as usual, because you still need to reject moves in the other dimensions. But it takes a long long time to figure out that you've radically underestimated the scale of one of the dimensions, because you're moving so slowly in that dimension.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rats comparisons
parts:
Definitely incorporating information from the whole trajectory is worth doing—I think that sort of effect is part of the reason that the step size tuning is better for NUTS than for HMC.

A possible quick fix would be to do a quick MAP point estimate (on transformed variables to avoid at least the most common degeneracies) to get an initial state. That should reduce the effect where giant moves caused by poor initialization get misinterpreted when estimating variances. I'm sure there are situations where it'll break, though.

Another option would be to only do these transformations after burn-in. Then we wouldn't be able to get the benefits during burn-in, but maybe those benefits aren't actually realizable during burn-in by any scheme, since by definition you can't estimate the shape of a distribution with pre-burn-in samples.

Matt
